Grades used throughout: VERIFIED means a primary document (filing, court order, executed agreement, SEC release) states it. text:
There are two schools of thought on how markets work.

Efficient markets: participants are rational, and all known information is already in the price.

Irrational markets: cognitive biases like overreaction, underreaction, herding, loss aversion and anchoring push prices away from fair value.

Those mispricings persist. Momentum, pre/post-earnings drift, bubbles and crashes all come from them, and limits to arbitrage keep rational traders from fully closing the gap.

There is a pre earnings drift in NVDA and that gap should close prior to earnings. 

That gap is where we do our work.

text:
$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE WHY NVIDIA HAS NO SIDE B OR SIDE C: THE UNDERWRITING QUESTION

The obvious question after the Financial Times reported that Nvidia carries up to $900 million of Side A only D&O insurance, with no Side B and no Side C, is why a company of this size would leave its own balance sheet uninsured. The answer being whispered is that the company could not have survived the diligence: that applying for entity coverage would have exposed what was going on inside.

That theory gets the mechanism wrong, and the correct mechanism is more interesting. D&O underwriters do not investigate anybody. What applying for Side B and Side C actually requires is a signature: a set of representations, made after polling the board and the executive team, about what the company and its officers know. Here is what that process involves, what differs between the three sides of the policy, and what follows for Nvidia.

WHAT UNDERWRITERS ACTUALLY DO

An underwriter pricing a large public company's D&O program works from paper and public data. The broker assembles a submission: the application, the last twelve months of SEC filings, and the indemnification provisions of the charter and bylaws. The carrier reviews financials, claims history, market capitalization, share volatility, credit spreads, ownership concentration, and litigation history, benchmarks the company against peers, and models securities claim frequency and severity. On large placements there is a management presentation

-> Make Your Product Cheaper.  Potentially, Much Much Cheaper.

Then agents will use it more.  Agents measure and track everything.  Humans buy a product and sort of … forget.  Not entirely, but partially, until we get a shocking bill and yet another price increase for the renewal cycle.

Not agents.  If your product is too expensive, they stop using you as much.  If it’s not cost effective, they seek out another solution. Right now.  That day. 

We’ve ditching apps that our agents couldn’t use as often as they needed to.  We ditched Marketo, and we’ve moving off even of our own core AI products now, because they just make it too expensive per API call, per usage, etc.

Agents will use your product far more than humans, if you do it right.

So you have to make it cheaper.

Many, many will resist.

Most stocks do not go up in a straight line. They go up, they fall apart, and then they go up again — and the fall is where the money is made, if the story is still true.

$PLTR went to $45 in early 2021. Then it fell to $7-8, and the bottom printed near $6. More than an 80% drawdown. Everyone wrote it off. The business kept building — government contracts, then commercial, then AI — and the stock went to $207. Then it fell again, nearly 50%, to about $107. And then it went to $209.

text:
$SPCX - SpaceX aborted its Super Heavy booster catch attempt during Friday's 15th Starship test flight, diverting the rocket offshore, where it flipped and exploded in the ocean. The setback complicates Elon Musk's goal of making Starship fully reusable.

* Booster Failure: Launch and stage separation succeeded, but mission control canceled the catch just over five minutes into flight. SpaceX has not identified the cause.

* Starship Mission: The upper stage reached orbit and is scheduled to complete 14 orbits over 22 hours, deploy 26 V3 Starlink satellites and return to Starbase for its first catch attempt.

* Reusability: SpaceX has caught Super Heavy boosters three times but has never caught Starship's upper stage. Flight 15 was intended to recover both stages for the first time.

* Expansion Plans: Starship is central to NASA contracts, proposed orbital AI data centers and Moon and Mars missions. Musk targets more frequent launches next year, supported by a planned Louisiana launch site.

text:
I've seen a lot of commentary around $SE sales & marketing spend, but I think it's worth putting the numbers into context.

A few things stand out:

1. The relationship isn't always immediate. 
In Q3 2023, incremental S&M spend increased by $424m against $215m of incremental revenue. The following quarter, incremental revenue rose to $306m while incremental S&M spend fell to just $49m. There can clearly be a lag.

2. Look at the latest numbers. 
In Q2 2026, incremental revenue was $690m against $246m of incremental S&M. In Q3, that improved to $795m against $227m. That's $3.50 of incremental revenue for every additional dollar of S&M.

3. Monetisation and GMV growth aren't mutually exclusive. 
Higher take rates are positive, but sustainability depends on maintaining competitive seller economics and consumer value.

For me, the question isn't simply how much $SE is spending on S&M, but what return it's generating. The latest numbers suggest the investment is translating into meaningful revenue growth.

text:
$MSOS, the largest cannabis ETF, is the tail that wags the dog of weed stocks.
It might be the worst thing that has ever happened to cannabis investors as...
It is a liquid ETF comprised of illiquid cannabis equities.
That is a toxic combination that rarely has a good ending - regardless of the industry that the ETF might serve.
Unfortunately, what has made matters worse has been (an arguably) poorly executed allocation strategy of the portfolio manager. (A good example of this was the misallocation of (selling) $GTBIF (our favorite stock in the sector) and using the proceeds to buy $GLAS)  Note: The guy that first understood that $MSOS could be value destructive to cannabis investors was the CEO of $GTBIF @Bkov9 - but few listened to his protestations.
Now $MSOS has a near $30 million debit balance (ergo it is on margin) because of the aforementioned portfolio strategy and recent redemptions.
This saddens me as it has hurt investors in a space that has promise because of a changing and improving regulatory landscape (leading to a more equitable tax situation among other factors), stable industry fundamentals and an improving quality of company managements.  
At some point in time the schism between upside opportunity and the current $MSOS share price will provide a unique opportunity - even despite the $MSOS headwind.
Unfortunately (again), many retail investors have been decimated before this has occurred - and have not been able to hold on to their investments in cannabis.

text:
Out of all the AI earnings I've seen this year, $IREN's were among the best by far. The presentation was easily my favourite. It made the business so much easier to follow as an investor.

At roughly $8bn, the market cap makes no sense next to what IREN has built.

It has $5.8bn of cash, $6bn of data centre assets with a 20 year useful life and a $20.3bn backlog, two thirds of it with investment grade counterparties. More customer prepayments are still to come in, with the newest five year contract prepaying 90% of the GPU capex.

Add the debt, take off the cash, and you're paying roughly $12bn for the whole business. That's about 3x the $4bn+ ARR targeted for January.

Of course, understanding the business doesn't mean we can predict everything affecting the stock. For example, no deep dive into IREN could have predicted Jensen's affair and resignation.

But out of all the neo's, I think IREN is the best right now.
